newsitem.title: USA: EMI to cut more North American jobs in restructuring.
newsitem.headline: EMI to cut more North American jobs in restructuring.

text.p: EMI Group Plc will soon announce more job cuts as part of a restructuring of North American music operations to cut costs and boost the group's market share in the $40 billion global music market.

A company spokeswoman said on Thursday that an announcement relating to the final phase of a restructuring announced in late May would be made by either Friday or Monday after management had notified affected employees.

The latest round of job cuts, estimated to total around 135 people at its EMI Records and Enclave labels, will significantly reduce the music company's East Coast presence, a source near the company said.

The EMI spokeswoman reiterated that the restructuring is expected to save up to around 40 million pounds annually ($65.6 million) by next year, although industry sources said annual savings could actually hit $100 million.
EMI, whose roster of artists ranges from The Beatles to the now-popular Spice Girls, forecast only modest progress this year in the face of a subdued music market.

Nevertheless, it has recently staged a comeback in current U.S. album market share year-to-date to rate third among the giant labels, including Time Warner's Warner Music, Seagram Co. Ltd's Universal Music Group, PolyGram NV, Sony Corp. and Bertelsmann.

EMI, which had sales of $5.9 billion last year, is the only major music company not part of a larger group and has long been seen as a takeover target. Several industry sources have speculated that the restructuring is driven by a desire to trim EMI down so that it is more attractive to suitors.
Rumours have persisted that Seagram and EMI have held preliminary merger negotiations, but EMI Chairman Sir Colin Southgate flatly denied these rumours last month. Seagram has declined to comment.

The latest cutbacks at EMI come less than a month after a shakeup that saw the departure of Charles Koppelman, chairman of EMI's North American division, and Terri Santisi, the division's executive vice president, closure of the New York corporate office and dismissal of more than a dozen employees.

As part of the restructuring announced in May, the company promoted Ken Berry, who headed EMI Music International and the Virgin Records unit, to worldwide president of EMI Recorded Music, with added control of the EMI Capitol label.
Sources said Berry met with label executives this week to discuss budgets and cost cuts.

"On the day that we announced the restructuring, we said that Ken Berry would be undertaking a review of EMI labels. This announcement will be the final aspect of that restructuring," the spokeswoman said.
Industry sources said that some of the acts signed to the soon-to-be-shut EMI Records and Enclave labels will be transferred to the Capitol and Virgin labels.
Virgin is EMI's crown jewel, generating the bulk of its $5.9 billion in sales last year.
This year, hits from the Spice Girls and other Virgin acts like the Smashing Pumpkins, Scarface and Blur have helped boost EMI's sales.
